prompt: What sits between the hardware of a host and the instances running on it?
hint: The layer whose one job is to divide the machine.

choices.text: A hypervisor, which gives each guest its share and keeps the guests apart
choices.why: Right. It hands out threads, memory and virtual devices, and it is the wall between tenants.

choices.text: The host's operating system, whose kernel every instance on it shares
choices.why: That describes containers on one machine. Each instance boots its own operating system and kernel.

choices.text: A load balancer that sends each customer's traffic to their own share
choices.why: A load balancer spreads requests over instances; it does not divide a host's processors and memory.

choices.text: The security group, which walls each instance off from the others on the host
choices.why: A security group filters network traffic. The isolation of memory and processor between guests is the hypervisor's.

prompt: The provider tells you the host under your instance is being retired. What does that ask of you?
hint: Who owns the hardware, and what moves an instance to other hardware?

choices.text: Open a ticket so the provider's staff can replace the faulty parts in your server
choices.why: There is no server of yours to repair. The host is the provider's, and they retire it rather than fix it with you.

choices.text: Stop and start the instance, so that it lands on a different, healthy host
choices.why: Right. A stop releases the host and a start places the instance on another one, with its network volume still attached.

choices.text: Reinstall the operating system, since the new host runs a different hypervisor
choices.why: The guest does not depend on which host it lands on; the same image and disk boot on the next one.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because an instance never depends on any particular host
choices.why: It does depend on one while it runs; that is why the provider tells you. What is true is that you never pick the host.

prompt: Match each piece of the name c7gd.xlarge to what it says.
hint: Family, generation, attributes, size.

pairs.right: A Graviton processor, which is Arm

prompt: m7i.large and m7g.large both list 2 vCPU. What is different about those two vCPU?
hint: What a vCPU is on Intel and on Graviton.

choices.text: Nothing: a vCPU is a standard unit, so both give the same processor
choices.why: A vCPU is a hardware thread, and a thread is not the same amount of processor on every chip.

choices.text: The m7g has half the memory, which is how Arm types are made cheaper
choices.why: Both have 8 GiB on the sheet. The price difference comes from the processor, not from less memory.

choices.text: The m7i always runs its two at a higher clock, so it is the faster of the two
choices.why: Clock speed alone does not decide it, and the lesson says to measure because either one may win.

choices.text: On the m7i they are two threads of one core; on the m7g they are two cores
choices.why: Right. Intel cores run two threads each, and Graviton has one thread per core.

prompt: A service sits at 70% CPU from nine to six on a t3.medium left at its default settings. What is most likely happening?
hint: Which mode does a t3 launch in, and what does that mode do when the credits run out?

choices.text: It is held down to its baseline every afternoon, once the morning has used its credits
choices.why: That is standard mode. A t3 launches in unlimited mode unless somebody changed it.

choices.text: It keeps running at full speed and the surplus above its baseline is billed
choices.why: Right. In unlimited mode it spends past its credits and pays for the difference, which can cost more than a fixed type.

choices.text: Nothing extra: the hourly price of a t3 already includes any level of use
choices.why: The hourly price includes the baseline only. Use above it is paid for in credits or, in unlimited mode, in money.

choices.text: The provider moves it to a c7i.large, which has the same vCPU and memory
choices.why: No provider changes your instance type on its own; choosing a fixed type is your decision to make.

prompt: On Intel and AMD instance types, one vCPU is one hardware ___, and a physical core runs two of them.
hint: Simultaneous multithreading.

prompt: A t3.medium costs 0.06720 USD an hour on demand in sa-east-1. What does it cost for a month of 730 hours, in USD, to the cent?
hint: Hourly price times 730.

prompt: Why does the lesson turn hourly prices into months with 730 hours?
hint: Months are not all the same length.

choices.text: Providers bill every month as 30 days of 24 hours, which is 730 hours
choices.why: Thirty days of 24 hours is 720. Billing counts the hours actually used; 730 is an estimating convention.

choices.text: It is a 31-day month, so an estimate never comes out too low
choices.why: A 31-day month has 744 hours. 730 is the average, not the longest month.

choices.text: 8,760 hours a year over twelve: the average month
choices.why: Right, and it is the figure AWS's own pricing calculator uses.

choices.text: It leaves out a day of maintenance windows that is never billed
choices.why: Nothing is left out: 730 × 12 is exactly the 8,760 hours of a year.

prompt: In sa-east-1, which is cheaper per hour: two m7i.large or one m7i.xlarge?

choices.text: The two larges, because smaller sizes are priced lower per vCPU
choices.why: Per vCPU they are the same: each size step doubles the price with the processor.

choices.text: The xlarge, because one machine carries less overhead than two
choices.why: Whatever the overhead, the sheet charges exactly double for the xlarge.

choices.text: It depends on the month, because the xlarge is billed by the month and the larges by the hour
choices.why: Both are billed the same way, by the second on demand. The month is only how we estimate.

choices.text: Neither: 2 × 0.16065 is exactly 0.32130
choices.why: Right. The price is linear in size within a family, so the choice between them is about failure and software, not the rate.

prompt: On an m7i.xlarge (4 vCPU, 16 GiB) a service peaks at 3 GiB of memory and averages 15% CPU over a month. What is the sensible next step?
hint: Memory is the hard limit; is it close?

choices.text: Move to an m7i.large and measure again next month
choices.why: Right. Both numbers fit the smaller size comfortably, and a month later you check that they still do.

choices.text: Keep the xlarge, because memory is a hard limit and must never be cut
choices.why: It is a hard limit, which is why the peak has to fit. A 3 GiB peak fits in 8 GiB with plenty to spare.

choices.text: Move it to a t3.micro, the cheapest line on the sheet
choices.why: A t3.micro has 1 GiB. The 3 GiB peak would not fit, and memory is the limit that breaks things.

choices.text: Move it to a memory-optimised type, since memory is what matters most here
choices.why: That family gives more memory per vCPU, which is the opposite of what 3 GiB out of 16 is asking for.

prompt: Match each field of the run-instances request to what it decides.
hint: Six answers every launch needs.

pairs.right: The disk the instance boots from
Its network, and on AWS its zone
The public SSH key placed on it

prompt: aws ec2 describe-instances, run with an empty environment, printed NoCredentials. What does that tell you?
hint: A request to AWS has to be signed.

choices.text: AWS received the request and refused it because the account has no instances
choices.why: An empty account answers with an empty list. This error came from the laptop, before any request was sent.

choices.text: The CLI had nothing to sign the request with, so nothing was sent to AWS
choices.why: Right. The CLI refused locally; the course never sends a request anywhere.

choices.text: describe-instances is not available in sa-east-1
choices.why: It is a basic call in every region. The error names credentials, not the region.

choices.text: The CLI version is too old to talk to EC2 and has to be upgraded first
choices.why: The same CLI generated the EC2 skeleton a moment earlier. It knows EC2; it had no identity.

prompt: The skeleton from --generate-cli-skeleton shows "InstanceType": "a1.medium". What should you make of that?
hint: Where did the skeleton come from?

choices.text: It is the type AWS recommends for new accounts
choices.why: The skeleton knows nothing about accounts; it was built on the laptop with no account at all.

choices.text: The CLI read it from the default type configured in your account
choices.why: The CLI ran with no credentials and no configuration, so it read nothing from any account.

choices.text: Nothing: it is a placeholder the CLI writes into an example request
choices.why: Right. The skeleton is built from the API description the CLI ships with, and the value only shows where a type goes.

choices.text: It is the smallest type that can use the other fields of the request
choices.why: Any type can use those fields. The value was not chosen for a reason; it fills a slot.

prompt: What is a machine image?
hint: What is copied when an instance is launched?

choices.text: A list of packages that cloud-init installs on the first boot
choices.why: That is user data. An image is the disk itself, before anything runs at boot.

choices.text: A copy of a running instance's memory, so that it resumes where it left off
choices.why: An image is a disk, and an instance launched from it boots from scratch.

choices.text: The hardware description of an instance type: its vCPU and memory
choices.why: That is the instance type, a separate choice in the launch request.

choices.text: A template for a boot disk, with an OS and what was installed
choices.why: Right. Launching copies it onto a new disk and boots from that.

prompt: A group that grew over a month now runs three different versions of nginx, and nobody chose that. What caused it?
hint: Which way of installing software depends on the day?

choices.text: User data that installs nginx at boot from the mirror
choices.why: Right. That is drift: configured at boot, machines launched on different days get different versions.

choices.text: nginx was baked into the golden image the group launches from
choices.why: A baked image holds fixed bytes, so every instance from it has the same version.

choices.text: The group spreads over zones, and each zone installs its own version
choices.why: Zones decide where machines run, not what is installed on them.

choices.text: The instances are on reserved pricing, which pins them to older software
choices.why: A pricing model changes the bill and nothing on the disk.

prompt: A team keeps five versions of a 20 GB golden image, each stored whole as snapshots at 0.0680 USD per GB-month in sa-east-1. What is the most they pay a month, in USD?
hint: Versions times size times the price.

prompt: A zone fails and the group launches replacements elsewhere, but the package mirrors are unreachable for an hour. Which replacements start serving?
hint: What does each approach need from outside the instance at boot?

choices.text: All of them, because the provider keeps a copy of every mirror inside each zone
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson promises that, and the question says the mirrors cannot be reached.

choices.text: The ones configured at boot, because they fetch the newest version of everything
choices.why: They are the ones that need the mirrors. They boot, then wait on installs that cannot finish.

choices.text: The ones from a baked image, since they need nothing outside themselves to start
choices.why: Right. That is the second row of the table, and it matters on exactly the day things are failing.

choices.text: None of them, since no instance can boot while a mirror is down
choices.why: Booting needs only the image. The mirrors matter only to a machine that installs at boot.

prompt: What tells cloud-init that user data is a configuration file rather than a script?
hint: Look at the first line of web.yaml.

choices.text: The .yaml extension of the file you pass at launch
choices.why: User data reaches the instance as text with no file name. The first line is what cloud-init reads.

choices.text: A first line that says #cloud-config
choices.why: Right. A text starting with #! is run as a script instead.

choices.text: A key named format: yaml at the top of the file
choices.why: There is no such key; cloud-init decides from the first line.

choices.text: A first line that says #!/bin/bash
choices.why: That marks a shell script, the other form cloud-init accepts.

prompt: Put what web.yaml does on the first boot in the order cloud-init does it.
hint: Users in the first stage; the rest in the last one.
items: The user ana is created with her SSH key
runcmd puts the hostname into the page
trap: Writing the file before installing nginx is what defer: true prevents.

prompt: A cloud-config says ssh_authorised_keys instead of ssh_authorized_keys. What happens when an instance boots with it?
hint: Does cloud-init refuse, or warn?

choices.text: The instance refuses to boot until the file is fixed
choices.why: cloud-init treats schema problems as warnings at boot. The machine comes up regardless.

choices.text: cloud-init recognises the British spelling and installs the key anyway
choices.why: The schema check refused exactly that spelling; the key it knows is spelt with a z.

choices.text: It boots with a warning in its log, and without the key
choices.why: Right, which can leave you unable to log in to read that log. That is why the file is checked first.

choices.text: The provider rejects the launch request because the user data is invalid
choices.why: The provider stores user data as text and does not read it. Only cloud-init, inside the instance, does.

prompt: To wait for the first boot to finish and learn whether cloud-init failed, you run: cloud-init ___ --wait
hint: One word, the state of the run.

prompt: A team wants to put the database password in the user data of its launch template. What is wrong with that?
hint: Who can read user data back?

choices.text: Nothing, because user data is encrypted and only cloud-init can read it
choices.why: It is not kept from anybody on the instance: the metadata service hands it to any process there.

choices.text: The password would be reset at every reboot, because user data runs on each start
choices.why: The modules in the lesson run once per instance. The problem is who can read it, not how often.

choices.text: cloud-init would print the password to the console on every boot
choices.why: Nothing in the file asks for that. The exposure is quieter: the text can simply be read back.

choices.text: Anyone on the instance, or allowed to describe it, reads it
choices.why: Right. Fetching the secret at boot from the provider's secret store, with a role, keeps it out of the template.

prompt: Match each action to what happens to the instance's disks.
hint: A reboot stays on the host; a stop leaves it.

pairs.right: Both kinds of disk keep their data
The instance store is erased; the root volume waits
The root volume goes too, unless you said otherwise

right_distractors: The root volume is erased and the instance store kept

prompt: An instance with a 50 GB gp3 root volume in sa-east-1 is stopped and forgotten. gp3 is 0.1520 USD per GB-month. What does it still cost a month, in USD?
hint: The processor stops charging; the volume does not.

prompt: Overnight a group replaced one of its instances. A report a colleague had generated by hand into /home/ubuntu on it is gone. What went wrong?
hint: What does a replacement keep?

choices.text: The group should have copied the home directory onto the replacement
choices.why: A group never copies anything from the old instance. The replacement comes from the image.

choices.text: Something only one machine held was kept on an instance the group was free to replace
choices.why: Right: a pet among cattle. The replacement keeps what is in the image and nothing written since.

choices.text: The report was on the instance store, and a network volume would have kept it
choices.why: The root volume of the old instance is deleted with it on termination, and the new one starts from the image either way.

choices.text: The group should have stopped and started the instance rather than replacing it
choices.why: Replacing is what a group does with an unhealthy instance; it does not nurse one back.

prompt: Servers that are numbered, built from an image and replaced rather than repaired are called ___; the ones set up by hand and nursed back to health are pets.
hint: The other half of the phrase.

prompt: In sa-east-1, m7g.large is 0.13010 USD an hour on demand and 0.08060 on a one-year reservation with no upfront. What is the reservation's discount, in percent, to one decimal place?
hint: 1 − reserved / on demand.

prompt: In sa-east-1 a t3.medium is 0.06720 USD an hour on demand and 0.03860 reserved for a year. Above what share of the year's hours, in percent, does the reservation become the cheaper choice?
hint: The reservation is owed for every hour; on demand only for the hours used.

prompt: Which of these fits spot capacity?
hint: The provider may take it back with two minutes' warning.

choices.text: The only database server of a small shop
choices.why: An interruption would take the shop's data offline, or worse. Spot is for work that can be dropped.

choices.text: A group of one that must always bring the website back
choices.why: The group would bring it back, but on spot it may be reclaimed at any moment and often.

choices.text: A queue of video conversions where a lost job is simply retried
choices.why: Right. Work that checkpoints or retries loses a little time when interrupted, and nothing else.

choices.text: The machine that keeps every user's session in its own memory, all day
choices.why: Reclaiming it would log everybody out at once; sessions belong somewhere that outlives the machine.

prompt: A team expects to move its servers from m7i to m7g halfway through the year. Which commitment keeps its discount after the move?
hint: One promise names a machine, the other an amount of spending.

choices.text: A savings plan of the kind that covers any instance family
choices.why: Right. It commits to spending per hour, and the discount applies to whatever matching machines run.

choices.text: A one-year reservation for m7i.large, which moves with the workload
choices.why: A reservation names a type. After the move nothing runs as m7i.large, and the rate is still owed.

choices.text: Spot, since the discount there applies to any type
choices.why: Spot is not a commitment at all; it is capacity the provider can take back.

choices.text: A three-year reservation, which may be exchanged at no cost
choices.why: A longer term only makes the fixed promise longer. Nothing in the lesson says it can be swapped freely.

prompt: A group has min 2, desired 3 and max 6. One instance fails its health check. What does the group do?
hint: The group keeps a number true.

choices.text: Reboots the instance and waits to see if it recovers
choices.why: A group does not nurse an instance. It replaces it.

choices.text: Lowers desired to 2, since the minimum still allows it
choices.why: The failure does not change what was asked for. Desired stays 3 until a policy or a person changes it.

choices.text: Terminates it and launches a replacement from the template
choices.why: Right, and the count is back to three.

choices.text: Alerts an operator to log in and fix it
choices.why: Nobody is paged to log in: there should be nothing on it worth logging in for.

prompt: The web server process on one instance has crashed, but the virtual machine is running normally. Which health check notices?
hint: Which check asks the application?

choices.text: The provider's own check, since the instance is no longer doing its job
choices.why: That check asks whether the virtual machine runs and is reachable, and here it does and is.

choices.text: Both of them, one after the other
choices.why: Only one of them talks to the application. The other sees a healthy machine.

choices.text: Neither, because the grace period hides failures on running instances
choices.why: The grace period covers the first minutes after launch, not an instance that has been running.

choices.text: The load balancer's check, which requests a path from the application
choices.why: Right. It sees what users see, which is why a group serving web traffic should use it.

prompt: The setting that makes a group ignore health checks for a while after launching an instance is its health check ___ period.
hint: It gives a booting machine time.

prompt: A group tracks average CPU at a target of 50%. Six instances are averaging 75%. How many instances will it ask for?
hint: Current count × actual / target, rounded up.

prompt: A group tracks average CPU at 60%. Five instances are averaging 70%. How many instances will it ask for?
hint: There is no such thing as a fraction of a machine.

prompt: Put the steps between a rise in load and a new instance taking its share in order.
hint: The metric comes first; traffic comes last.
items: The metric is collected and the policy decides the rise is real
The group asks for instances and the provider places them
Each instance boots and runs its user data
The load balancer's health check passes
Traffic starts to reach the new instance
trap: Traffic reaches an instance only after its health check passes, not when it boots.

prompt: Why would a group track CPU at 50% rather than at 90%, which uses the machines better?
hint: What happens in the minutes before new instances serve?

choices.text: The headroom carries the load while new instances are on their way
choices.why: Right. At 90% every instance is saturated for the whole of the lag.

choices.text: Providers do not allow a target above 50%
choices.why: The target is yours to set. 90% is allowed; it is just a bad idea for a spiky load.

choices.text: At 90% the group would scale in too slowly and flap
choices.why: Flapping comes from scaling in too early, not from a high target.

choices.text: CPU readings above 50% are not reported to the policy until the next minute
choices.why: Readings are reported the same way at any level; the delay in collecting them is the same at 50 and 90.

prompt: Every Monday at 09:00 traffic triples within five minutes, and users see errors until about 09:10. What fixes it most directly?
hint: Which policy acts before the load arrives?

choices.text: Raise the maximum, so the group can add more machines
choices.why: The group is not stopping at its maximum; it is adding machines too late. A higher ceiling does not make them earlier.

choices.text: Shorten the health check grace period, so instances count sooner
choices.why: An instance that is not ready yet would fail its checks and be killed; the lag would not shrink.

choices.text: A scheduled action raising the minimum before 09:00 on Mondays
choices.why: Right. The load is predictable, so the clock can add the machines before it arrives.

choices.text: Switch from target tracking to step scaling, which reacts faster
choices.why: Both follow a metric, so both start after the load has already risen.

prompt: The nightly invoice job must run once a night while the group moves between 2 and 7 instances. What does that?
hint: Anything in the image runs on every member.

choices.text: Moving the cron line into the user data, so it only runs once
choices.why: User data runs once per instance, so seven instances would still mean seven runs.

choices.text: Keeping the cron job in the image, but setting min and max to 2
choices.why: Two instances in the image still send the invoices twice.

choices.text: One scheduler outside the group, or a shared lock
choices.why: Right. Something has to be the single place that decides the job runs.

choices.text: Nothing: the load balancer sends cron to only one instance
choices.why: A load balancer routes incoming requests. A cron job starts inside each machine and never passes through it.

prompt: An application moves from one instance to a group of three behind a load balancer. Which of these break? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which things live on one machine only?

choices.text: Logins kept in each process's memory
choices.why: The next request may reach another instance, which never saw the login.

choices.text: The nginx package baked into the image
choices.why: Every instance comes from the same image, so every one has it.

choices.text: Photos saved to /var/www/uploads
choices.why: A photo exists on the instance that received it, and nowhere else.

choices.text: A cron job in the image that e-mails the invoices
choices.why: Three instances run it three times, every night.

choices.text: A configuration file written by the user data
choices.why: User data runs on every new instance, so every one has the file.

prompt: Where should a group's instances keep users' sessions so that scaling in logs nobody out?
hint: Somewhere every instance can reach and none of them owns.

choices.text: On each instance's network volume, which outlives a stop
choices.why: A replacement starts from the image, and the old root volume goes with the terminated instance.

choices.text: In a managed database or cache shared by every instance
choices.why: Right. The session outlives any one machine, and whichever instance gets the next request can read it.

choices.text: In the instance store, which is fast enough to hold them
choices.why: Speed is not the issue. The instance store belongs to the host and is gone at a stop.

choices.text: In the golden image, rebuilt every night
choices.why: An image holds what is the same for every machine. Sessions change every second.

prompt: A group replaces an instance. Which of these are still there afterwards? Choose all that apply.
hint: What lives in the image, and what lives off the instance?

choices.text: A configuration file somebody fixed over SSH last week
choices.why: Written by hand on one machine after it booted: not in the image, gone with the machine.

choices.text: An upload stored in object storage
choices.why: It never lived on the instance.

choices.text: The runtime baked into the golden image
choices.why: The replacement boots from the same image, so it has it.

choices.text: The log file of the instance that failed
choices.why: Logs written to its own disk go with it, unless they were shipped off as they were written.

choices.text: Rows in a managed database
choices.why: The database is run by the provider, apart from the group.

prompt: Match each way of buying an instance to what you promise in return.
hint: The discount is paid for with a promise.

pairs.right: To pay for one kind of instance for a term
To spend an amount per hour for a term
To give the machine back when asked

right_distractors: To run it at least 730 hours a month

prompt: Order these by on-demand price per hour in sa-east-1, cheapest first.
hint: Burstable is cheapest; Arm is cheaper than Intel at the same size; a size up doubles.
trap: m7g.large below m7i.large is the one people swap: same size, and the Graviton is cheaper.

prompt: A small shop runs its website on one instance and wants it to come back on its own if the machine fails, without paying for a second one. What fits?
hint: Which part of this lesson replaces a failed machine?

choices.text: A one-year reservation, which guarantees the instance is always running
choices.why: A reservation is a price. It says nothing about replacing a machine that fails.

choices.text: A t3 in unlimited mode, so it never runs out of processor
choices.why: That is about CPU credits. A failed machine stays failed whatever its mode.

choices.text: A spot instance, since the provider gives it back after an interruption
choices.why: The provider takes spot capacity back; it promises nothing about returning it.

choices.text: A group of one, with the data kept off the instance
choices.why: Right. The group replaces its one machine, and the data survives because it was never on it.

prompt: Machines launched on different days that were meant to be identical and are not have suffered configuration ___.
hint: The word the images section uses.
